newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's capital shut down by opposition protest.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's capital shut down by opposition protest.

text.p: Zaire's capital Kinshasa, final goal of Laurent Kabila's rebels, was virtually shut down by an opposition stay-at-home protest on Wednesday.

The usually bustling streets of the city of five million were practically empty as the protest, called by the opposition to demand the end of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's reign, was largely followed.
Without fanfare Mobutu left Kinshasa for shipborne talks with Kabila off Congo, which many residents see as the last chance to avoid a bloody battle for the city.
Kabila, whose forces are closing in on Kinshasa, insists the only solution is for Mobutu to hand over power at the talks hosted by South African President Nelson Mandela.
Few people bothered to try to get to work. If they had tried there were no buses or taxis to take them.
Shops were shut in the city centre and even the market stalls, where Kinshasa's poorest residents scrape a daily living from petty trade, were largely deserted.

"The success of today's operation has clearly shown that the people don't want Mobutu any more, and people know exactly what to do when the rebels come," said Laurent Mbayo, an adviser to Mobutu's veteran political opponent Etienne Tshisekedi.
"People are surprised it has taken them (the rebels) so long to reach here," Mbayo told Reuters.
The protest was called by the political opposition before the government imposed a 10-hour overnight curfew on Kinshasa on Tuesday.
Photocopied sheets purporting to come from the rebels also told people to stay indoors.
With no fresh news from the battlefront, and only rumour to go on, people were left to speculate on what the future held.
On Tuesday reports reaching the city said teh rebels had taken a key bridge over the River Kwango and Mobutu's army had pulled back to Mbankana about 150 km (90 miles) from the city.
"We are not afraid, the people are prepared, we know the rebels are our brothers and are not coming here to kill us," said car mechanic Baudoin Menga.
The rebel alliance has been welcomed across Zaire by people tired after over three decades of Mobutu's rule that have made the potentially rich country at the heart of Africa destitute and corrupt.
But fears of trouble are heightened in Kinshasa by the knowledge that after being driven from three quarters of the sprawling state, Mobutu's soldiers have nowhere left to run.
Hundreds of people were killed in two rounds of looting led by soldiers in 1991 and 1993.
"The danger doesn't come from the rebels, it comes from the army," said Mbayo.
More than 4,000 troops from the United States, Belgium, Britain, France and Portugal are on standby in Congo and off the Atlantic coast to step in and rescue their nationals if there is trouble.
